nameStory: The Northern Spurred Woodland Funnelweaver gets its name from the distinctive spurs (small projections) on the male's legs and its preference for wooded habitats in northern regions. Like all funnelweavers, it creates sheet webs with a funnel-shaped retreat where it waits to ambush prey that stumble onto its silken platform.
description: This medium-sized spider is a master architect of sheet webs, building flat silk platforms with a distinctive funnel retreat in one corner. The Northern Spurred Woodland Funnelweaver has a brownish body with long, sturdy legs that help it race across its web to capture prey. Adults typically measure about half an inch in body length, with females being slightly larger than males. This species prefers the cool, moist environments of northern woodlands.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for a flat, sheet-like web with a distinctive funnel or tube-shaped retreat at one edge, often built close to the ground among fallen logs or rocks

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated, somewhat flattened body with a brownish coloration and relatively long, robust legs that feel sturdy to the touch if handled gently

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Sits motionless in the funnel opening, then darts out lightning-fast when prey touches the web before quickly retreating back to safety

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length around half an inch, with legs extending the overall size to about 1-1.5 inches across when at rest

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight small, dark eyes arranged in two rows, giving the spider decent vision for detecting movement on and around its web

habitat: Found in cool, moist woodlands throughout northern New England, particularly in areas with plenty of fallen logs, rock crevices, and leaf litter. They prefer the understory of mixed or coniferous forests where humidity remains high and there's abundant ground-level structure for web attachment. Look for their webs in the spaces between rocks, under log overhangs, or in the root systems of large trees.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and begin rebuilding webs in prime locations. Mating activity increases as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak web-building season with fully developed sheet webs most visible. Adults are most active and easiest to spot in their funnel retreats.
seasonality.fall: Egg-laying occurs and webs may become more tattered. Adults prepare for winter by seeking protected overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Spiders retreat deep into crevices, under bark, or into thick leaf litter where they remain largely inactive until spring.

funFact: When prey lands on their sheet web, these spiders can detect the exact location through vibrations transmitted through the silk and reach their target in less than a second, making them some of the fastest ambush predators in the forest floor ecosystem.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with grass spiders, but woodland funnelweavers build their webs among rocks and logs rather than in open grassy areas. Remember: 'Woodland webs in woody places, grass spider webs in grassy spaces.'
contextualKnowledge: With only 2 recorded observations in New England, this species appears to be quite rare in the region or possibly at the southern edge of its range. Many funnel weaver species look very similar, making field identification challenging without close examination of specific anatomical features.
compareHints: The Northern Spurred Woodland Funnelweaver can be distinguished from its Coras relatives primarily by the male's distinctive leg spurs and its preference for higher elevation, cooler woodland habitats. Other Coras species may prefer different microhabitats like cave entrances or more exposed rocky areas, though all share the characteristic funnel web architecture.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Distinguishing Coras medicinalis from its close relatives like Coras lamellosus or the Northern Spurred Woodland Funnelweaver requires examining fine details of body structure that are difficult to see in the field.
Distinguishing between different Coras species requires close examination of anatomical features that are difficult to see in the field.
Distinguishing Coras juvenilis from its close relatives like Coras medicinalis or Coras montanus requires expert examination of reproductive structures and other microscopic features.
Coras aerialis is virtually indistinguishable in the field from its relatives like Coras medicinalis and Coras montanus without examining reproductive structures under magnification.
